summary:
Angola decriminalised same-sex conduct with effect from 11 February 2021. The statute adopted in 2019 overturned the colonial-era provision that described same-sex relationships as a 'vice against nature', and in the same instrument made discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation punishable by imprisonment in employment and services. A continental overview published in October 2019 rated Angola as having gone furthest among the African reforms of that period, both by removing the colonial offence and by attaching penalty to orientation-based discrimination.

Constitutional protection is weaker than the statutory position. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre's chapter on transgender rights in Angola records that Article 23 of the Constitution does not list gender or sexual orientation among the prohibited grounds of discrimination, while the rights to identity, privacy, liberty, protection from torture and expression are located across Title II of the same document. A trans visitor therefore has statutory recourse against orientation-based discrimination but no enumerated constitutional ground covering gender.

No specific law permits transgender people to change their gender marker on identity documents or passports. Section 78 of the Código do Registo Civil 2015 states in general that details entered into registration records should not be altered, but section 87 gives the Civil Registrar broad authority to make changes, including changes of name and changes where altered facts affect a person's legal identity and status, so a marker change may be pursued through that section. Whether registrars apply section 87 to gender changes in practice is not documented in the sources.

Angola provides no legal recognition to same-sex couples, and social pressure to marry a partner of the opposite sex is significant. National news magazines described an unofficial same-sex commitment ceremony held in 2005 as 'shameless' and 'abominable'. People living with HIV are legally entitled to health care services and to protection from discrimination in employment. The sources record no shelters, safe houses, gender-neutral facilities or other dedicated facilities for LGBTQ people anywhere in the country.

Documentation of current conditions comes from Angolan organisations themselves. A shadow report on Angola's compliance with the African Charter, submitted for the African Commission's 81st session in Banjul in October and November 2024 by Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, I am Trans Movement, ASTA, Diversidade Masculina and others with ILGA and Synergia support, documents human-rights violations against LGBTQI+ people. A separate submission by Angolan LGBTQI+ organisations to the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights raised discrimination and health-access issues affecting lesbian, bisexual, transgender, intersex and queer people ahead of Angola's review at the Committee's 74th session.
tangentialFactors:
Visible trans presence in Angolan public life predates decriminalisation by nearly a decade. In April 2012 the BBC profiled kuduro singer Titica, born male and presenting female, as a mainstream star at 25, in a profile describing Angola as a Catholic country where homosexuality was then illegal and punishable by hard labour. The same reporting noted that homosexuality remained criminal at that time, so the coexistence of a prominent trans figure and a functioning offence is established rather than inferred.

A 2017 ILGA poll found that 49% of Angolans believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender. Two LGBT organisations operate in Angola, of which only the Iris Angola Association holds official legal recognition, granted by the Angolan Justice Ministry in June 2018; at that time it had around 200 members, based in Luanda with offices in Benguela and Lubango. The three major political parties have not addressed LGBT issues in their platforms. In 2010 the Angolan government refused to receive the openly gay incoming Israeli ambassador, Isi Yanouka, reportedly because of his sexual orientation; this was a diplomatic reception decision rather than a rule affecting visas or entry.

Organisational infrastructure for LGBTQ Angolans remains thin. Education-focused work is nascent and underfunded: the first association, Acção Humana, launched in 2006 but has been unable to obtain funding, and efforts to develop educational programmes specifically for LGBT people have struggled to secure NGO support. An HIV/AIDS educational programme for LGBT people is only beginning to develop through NGOs including Population Services International, and a 2007 study estimated that roughly five percent of HIV infections were among men who have sex with men. Some charities have begun working with LGBT community members on HIV/AIDS education under the tolerance extended to non-governmental organisations generally.
localsOnly:
Trans Angolans seeking a legal gender change must work through the civil registration system rather than a dedicated procedure. Section 78 of the Código do Registo Civil 2015 discourages alteration of registered details, while section 87 vests the Civil Registrar with authority to make changes where a change of facts alters a person's legal identity and status, which is the provision on which a gender-marker application would rest.

People living with HIV carry enforceable entitlements in Angola: health care services and protection against discrimination in employment. Civil-society organisations serving LGBTQ communities operate under general NGO law, with the Justice Ministry responsible for recognition; Iris Angola Association received that recognition in June 2018. Community programming for LGBTQ people, particularly education and HIV prevention work, depends on external NGO funding that has not been secured for several initiatives since Acção Humana launched in 2006.
outOfScopeNotes:
No entry or visa provisions for Angola are recorded in the source inventory. The only entry-adjacent material is external: reference links to Asylumlaw.org's 'Sexual Minorities & HIV Status (Angola)' asylum information packets, and local-laws-and-customs travel advice published by the UK Foreign & Commonwealth Office. Whether border officials screen or question arriving travellers on the basis of gender presentation is unresolved and not sourced.

Whether section 87 of the 2015 civil registration code has been used to change a legal gender in practice is not documented; the sources describe it as a possible route only. The inventory carries no findings on youth or minors, on medication or continuity of care for travellers, or on education access. Dedicated LGBTQ facilities are recorded as absent, but the sources do not state whether this reflects a survey with national coverage or the limits of available reporting.
